uncited: The AABB Ray Intersection method computes the entry ($t_{min}$) and exit ($t_{max}$) distances of a ray against an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), returning a boolean hit status.
It solves the fundamental problem of determining whether a ray intersects a volume primitive and, if so, the interval along the ray parameter $t$ where the intersection occurs.

It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the "slab" method (computing intersections with min/max planes per axis) and its common implementation as a batched kernel for GPU acceleration, whereas [Ray-Bounding Box Intersection and Sampling Preparation](2364-ray-bounding-box-intersection-and-sampling-preparation.md) focuses on sampling preparation and [Ray-Cube Intersection](2466-ray-cube-intersection.md) assumes unit cubes.
*   AABBs: $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 6}$, where each row is $[x_{min}, y_{min}, z_{min}, x_{max}, y_{max}, z_{max}]$.
**Compute Slab Intersections:** For each axis $i \in \{x, y, z\}$, calculate the intersection distances with the min and max planes of the AABB.
Let $\mathbf{B}_{min} = [x_{min}, y_{min}, z_{min}]$ and $\mathbf{B}_{max} = [x_{max}, y_{max}, z_{max}]$.
A pure PyTorch implementation of the slab method.
It is functionally identical to the CUDA kernel but slower due to lack of specialized hardware instructions and memory coalescing.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot M)$ for $N$ rays and $M$ AABBs, with a very small constant factor (6 subtractions, 6 multiplications, 6 comparisons per pair).
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N \cdot M)$ to store the output tensors $t_{min}, t_{max}, hit$.
*   **Limitations:** Does not handle rotated boxes (use [Ray-OBB Intersection Test](6603-ray-obb-intersection-test.md) instead).
It is a direct application of the separating axis theorem for axis-aligned boxes.
